episodes.title: Is our national debt finally too much? (update)
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Planet Money revisits the US national debt debate, tracing it from the 2009 stimulus-era arguments through the influential (and later discredited) Reinhart-Rogoff "90% of GDP" threshold paper, and updates it with 2026 commentary from economists Karen Dynan and Kenneth Rogoff. The core shift: economists who once dismissed debt concerns are now turning hawkish as US Treasury yields have risen sharply, changing the calculus on debt sustainability for the world's benchmark risk-free asset.

**Key points**
- US gross national debt has crossed $40 trillion, up from ~$6-11 trillion in 2008-2012.
- The 2010 Reinhart-Rogoff paper claimed debt above 90% of GDP roughly halves growth; a 2013 spreadsheet error weakened but didn't overturn the correlation.
- Congress passed large tax cuts in 2025 that reduced revenue; debt service now exceeds $1 trillion/year, a record.
- The 10-year US Treasury yield recently hit its highest level since just before the Great Recession.
- CBO projects debt will cross 120% of GDP by 2036, higher than any prior point including WWII.
- Karen Dynan, a former dove, now calls herself a "debt hawk"; Kenneth Rogoff maintains his long-held hawkish stance and sees >50% odds of a significant debt-related shock.
- Both cite AI-driven investment buildout and geopolitical shocks (Iran war) as complicating factors for gauging debt tolerance.

**FX / rates implications**
- Rising UST yields and deteriorating US fiscal trajectory are a global anchor: higher US term premia typically pressure DXY higher and tighten financial conditions, a headwind for EM carry trades and capital flows into EM Asia/LATAM.
- Persistent US fiscal deficits risk keeping US rates structurally higher, reducing the rate differential appeal of EM local-currency debt unless EM central banks maintain premium carry.
- A future US debt/rates shock (flagged by Rogoff/Dynan as a real tail risk) would likely trigger broad risk-off, hitting high-beta EM FX (BRL, COP, ZAR-like proxies, IDR) hardest.

**Watch list**
- US 10-year Treasury yield trajectory and any further spike toward pre-Great Recession highs.
- CBO debt/GDP projections (120% by 2036) versus actual fiscal trajectory under 2025 tax cuts.
- US interest expense as a share of budget (already >$1 trillion/year) — further increases could force fiscal adjustment (spending cuts/tax hikes) with knock-on effects for global rates and USD.
